title: Plan repository code-reduction audit
instructions:
Plan an initiative to reduce this project's maintained code size and unused code paths while preserving intended behavior. This is a planning-only meta job: design a subsequent repository audit job, not the cleanup itself.

Read the repository instructions and relevant package documentation first. Inspect the repository's structure, module registration, public entry points, dependency boundaries, and test/verification setup enough to ground the plan in actual files. Separate maintained project code from generated state, vendored dependencies, and runtime artifacts; exclude the latter from cleanup scope. Do not perform an exhaustive audit at this stage.

Design an audit that identifies genuinely unused code paths, obsolete compatibility branches, duplicated logic, unnecessary wrappers, and complexity that can be removed without replacing it with larger abstractions. Prefer meaningful reductions in maintained implementation and branching, not formatting tricks, compressed code, or deletion of useful tests, documentation, or supported features. Account for Emacs Lisp dynamic dispatch, hooks, advice, autoloads, interactive commands, keybindings, macros, conditional module loading, configuration-driven references, and external consumers. Missing static references alone are not evidence that code is unused. Treat uncertain reachability or undocumented support requirements as questions, not deletion recommendations.

Return a self-contained Markdown planning report in your response containing: (1) the repository map and scope, with concrete paths and relevant verification commands; (2) phased audit work packages and their ordering; (3) an evidence checklist for each proposed finding, including location, behavior and callers, reachability analysis, rationale, estimated net code reduction, confidence, compatibility risk, verification, and unresolved questions; (4) prioritization criteria favoring low-risk, high-confidence simplification; (5) acceptance criteria and human review gates before any implementation; and (6) a ready-to-review prompt for a separate, read-only audit job that scans the repository and reports ranked, actionable findings without changing code. Mark any initial examples as preliminary leads rather than verified findings. Distinguish code reduction from the separate removal of behavior that may still be wanted.

Use the project's documented verification approach, including live Emacs checks where isolated compilation is unreliable, and identify checks requiring additional access or authorization. Plan verification rather than running state-changing checks now. State limitations and assumptions explicitly.

Do not edit or create files, delete code, install dependencies, change configuration, commit changes, or invoke live Emacs APIs. Do not create/import/run/schedule another job or change job stores, timing, evidence, or run history. Do not execute the proposed audit or cleanup. The deliverable is the plan and subsequent audit prompt only; execution requires separate user authorization.
